ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Wearing a plaid green A-line spring skirt from her new fashion line, paired with a black patent leather belt and black leather gladiator sandal stilettos, "Sex and the City" actress Kristin Davis is the perfect combination of sweet and fierce when we meet up after her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia. Kristin Davis surrounded by models and Belk store official Arlene Goldstein. It's a look that totally says her character, Charlotte, with a little bit of screen pal Carrie. Davis is so much like her character, adorable and upbeat, I expect Carrie or Samantha to drop in on our conversation and say something to shock her. As any true fan knows ... OK ... as every woman knows, watching "Sex and the City" was like being front row at a fashion show with a plot. TV show and movie costume designer Patricia Field dressed the characters in haute couture as they skipped down the streets of New York City in $600 stilettos. But is this reality? Most sane women wouldn't choose to walk even one city block in high heels. And most women certainly can't spend a month's rent on a belt or bag, even if they have a truly fabulous party to wear it to. So, what about us, the fashionistas on a budget? Are we to be ignored, forced to wear boring clothing and practical shoes? Luckily, no; designers are catching on. Target features affordable lines from high-end designers like Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. All of the pieces in Sarah Jessica Parker's clothing line Bitten cost less than $20 before the clothing store that carried them went under. Davis is the latest celebrity to jump on the clothing label bandwagon, designing a line for Belk department stores. Will she meet the same fate as Parker? Davis has the following to be successful. Although her character was by far the most conservatively dressed (Carrie strolling through town in just a bra top, anyone?), she had the most wearable wardrobe, and Davis became a fashion icon along with the rest of the ladies. Her favorite piece from her line? "I can't decide, impossible to choose!" she says. So I choose for her: definitely the gladiator heels. "It's important for women to have a strong shoe," she says. "Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you're good to go." She admits she didn't have a defined style before meeting Field, who bluntly told her that "Sexy Secretary" was going to be her look. Davis' philosophy is a good one: Stick with what works. She takes the look that Field defined for her "Sex and the City" character. Original it's not, but everything coming down the runway is something the stylish Charlotte York would definitely wear. Davis is in touch with all of us real women out there, saying, "I don't want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear." Her solution? Dresses, shoes and swimsuits worthy of a "Sex and the City" episode that you don't need Park Avenue pockets to afford. It's versatile enough to look good on every body type. "Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!" she says with a laugh. Davis won't spill any secrets from the scripts of the "Sex and the City" movie sequel, which comes out in May 2010, but she admits it's a "happy" movie. She does hint that our famous foursome might have to cut back a little on their clothing expenses as art imitates life. And she's willing to share some fashion tips: How to look like you stepped out of the wardrobe room on the set of the next "Sex and the City" movie? Green. "It's THE color" she says. And hey, who doesn't need to save some green? It all works out perfectly. I left the meeting with Davis to check out her displays. Then I skipped out into the streets of Atlanta, in a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals. That I got on sale, of course.

Keywords: ATLANTA, Georgia, CNN

outputs.L1:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — Wearing a plaid green A-line spring skirt from her new fashion line, cinched with a black patent leather belt and paired with black leather gladiator stiletto sandals, “Sex and the City” actress Kristin Davis is the perfect blend of sweet and fierce when we meet after her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia.

Kristin Davis, surrounded by models and Belk store official Arlene Goldstein, embodies a look that says her character Charlotte, with just a touch of onscreen pal Carrie. Davis is so much like her character — adorable and upbeat — that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to drop into our conversation and say something scandalous enough to shock her.

As any true fan knows ... OK, as every woman knows, watching “Sex and the City” was like sitting front row at a fashion show with a plot. Television and movie costume designer Patricia Field dressed the characters in haute couture as they strutted through the streets of New York City in $600 stilettos.

But is that reality? Most sensible women would not choose to walk even a single city block in high heels. And most women certainly cannot spend a month’s rent on a belt or bag, even if they have a truly fabulous party to attend.

So what about the rest of us — fashionistas on a budget? Are we to be ignored, left to wear boring clothes and practical shoes?

Fortunately, no. Designers are catching on. Target has featured affordable lines from high-end designers such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Every piece in Sarah Jessica Parker’s clothing line Bitten cost less than $20 before the clothing store that carried it went under.

Davis is the latest celebrity to join the clothing-label bandwagon, designing a line for Belk department stores. Will she meet the same fate as Parker?

Davis has the following to be successful. Although her character was by far the most conservatively dressed — Carrie strolling through town in just a bra top, anyone? — Charlotte had the most wearable wardrobe, and Davis became a fashion icon along with the rest of the ladies.

Her favorite piece from the line?

“I can’t decide, impossible to choose!” she says.

So I choose for her: definitely the gladiator heels.

“It’s important for women to have a strong shoe,” she says. “Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you’re good to go.”

She admits she did not have a defined style before meeting Field, who bluntly told her that “Sexy Secretary” was going to be her look.

Davis’ philosophy is a sound one: stick with what works. She has taken the look Field created for her “Sex and the City” character and made it her own. Original it may not be, but everything coming down the runway is something the stylish Charlotte York would unquestionably wear.

Davis is also in touch with all of us real women out there, saying, “I don’t want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear.”

Her solution? Dresses, shoes and swimsuits worthy of a “Sex and the City” episode — without requiring Park Avenue pockets to afford them. The line is versatile enough to flatter every body type.

“Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!” she says with a laugh.

Davis will not reveal any secrets from the script of the “Sex and the City” movie sequel, which comes out in May 2010, but she does admit it is a “happy” movie. She also hints that the famous foursome may have to cut back a little on clothing expenses as art imitates life.

And she is willing to share a few fashion tips. How can you look as though you stepped out of the wardrobe room on the set of the next “Sex and the City” movie?

Green.

“It’s THE color,” she says.

And really, who does not need to save some green? It all works out perfectly.

I left my meeting with Davis to check out her displays. Then I skipped out into the streets of Atlanta in a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals — which I got on sale, of course.
outputs.L2:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — When I meet Kristin Davis after her fashion presentation at the Belk department store in Atlanta, she is dressed in a green plaid A-line spring skirt from her new clothing collection, a black patent-leather belt, and black leather gladiator stiletto sandals. The “Sex and the City” star manages to look both charming and tough at the same time. Nearby, Davis is seen with models and Belk executive Arlene Goldstein.

The outfit feels very much like Charlotte, her famous character, with just a hint of Carrie mixed in. Davis herself is so cheerful and lovable — so Charlotte-like — that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to appear mid-interview and say something outrageous enough to make her blush.

As devoted fans know — or really, as most women know — watching “Sex and the City” often felt like sitting in the front row of a fashion show that happened to have a storyline. Costume designer Patricia Field put the women in high fashion as they moved through New York City wearing $600 stilettos.

But how realistic is that? Most reasonable women would not want to walk even a single city block in heels that high. And most women cannot pay the equivalent of a month’s rent for a handbag or belt, no matter how amazing the event is where they plan to wear it.

So where does that leave fashion lovers who have to watch their spending? Are we supposed to settle for dull outfits and sensible shoes?

Fortunately, the answer is no. Designers have begun to understand the demand. Target has offered lower-priced collections from major names such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Sarah Jessica Parker’s Bitten line featured items priced under $20 before the retailer that sold it closed.

Now Davis has become the newest celebrity to create a fashion label, launching a collection for Belk department stores. Could her line face the same fate as Parker’s? Davis seems to have the fan base needed to succeed. Although Charlotte was the most modestly dressed of the four women — remember Carrie walking around in little more than a bra top? — her wardrobe was also the easiest to imagine real women wearing. Along with the rest of the cast, Davis became a fashion figure.

When asked to name her favorite item from the collection, she refuses to choose.

“I can’t decide, impossible to choose!” she says.

So I pick for her: the gladiator heels, without question.

“It’s important for women to have a strong shoe,” Davis says. “Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you’re good to go.”

She acknowledges that before working with Patricia Field, she did not really have a clear personal style. Field, in her typically direct way, told Davis that “Sexy Secretary” would be her look.

Davis’ approach makes sense: find what works and stay with it. Her line borrows from the style Field created for Charlotte on “Sex and the City.” It may not be groundbreaking, but everything on the runway looks like something the polished Charlotte York would gladly wear.

Davis also seems aware of what regular women want. “I don’t want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear,” she says.

Her answer is a collection of dresses, shoes, and swimsuits that could fit naturally into a “Sex and the City” episode, without requiring a Park Avenue budget. The pieces are designed to be flexible and flattering on many different body shapes.

“Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!” she says, laughing.

Davis will not reveal any plot details from the script for the “Sex and the City” movie sequel, scheduled for release in May 2010, but she does describe it as a “happy” film. She also suggests that the famous foursome may have to reduce their fashion spending a bit, with art reflecting real life.

She is, however, happy to offer style advice. Want to look as though you just walked out of the wardrobe department for the next “Sex and the City” movie? Wear green.

“It’s THE color,” she says.

And really, who couldn’t use saving a little green, too? In the end, it all fits together perfectly.

After meeting Davis, I headed over to look at her displays. Then I stepped out onto the streets of Atlanta wearing a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals — which, naturally, I bought on sale.

That balance — aspirational but affordable — has become increasingly important in fashion retail. Not every fan can live like the women of “Sex and the City,” but many can still borrow a piece of the fantasy: a flattering dress, a feminine print, a little Charlotte-style composure on an ordinary day.

And in Atlanta, amid department-store racks and runway applause, Davis seemed to be selling more than clothes. She was selling the idea that elegance does not have to be exclusive — and that even without a Manhattan ZIP code, a woman can still dress like she has somewhere fabulous to go.

I meet Davis just after the show, where she has presented pieces from her new clothing line for Belk, a collection built around the idea that style should feel polished, feminine, and — most importantly — accessible.

“I wanted clothes that real women could wear,” Davis says as she smooths the front of a soft dress from the collection. “Pieces that feel pretty and put-together, but don’t require a Hollywood budget or a stylist standing next to you.”

That practicality is the heart of the line. The clothes have a romantic, easy elegance: printed dresses, flattering separates, cardigans, soft blouses, and pieces that can go from office to dinner without feeling overdone. Davis speaks about fashion not as a fantasy, but as something women live in — at work, at brunch, on dates, at school events, and in the everyday rush of life.

The Atlanta crowd seems to understand that immediately. Belk’s Southern audience responds warmly to wearable glamour, and Davis’s collection fits right into that world: feminine without being fussy, chic without being intimidating.

Of course, no conversation with Kristin Davis can completely avoid *Sex and the City*. The influence is there, not in a literal way, but in the spirit of dressing with personality. Charlotte’s classic femininity may echo through a few silhouettes, but Davis is clear that her own fashion vision is broader.

“*Sex and the City* taught us that clothes can tell a story,” she says. “But this line is about helping women tell their own stories.”

There are nods to the show’s legacy — a pretty dress that feels ready for lunch with friends, a polished jacket that could belong in a city apartment closet, a romantic print that recalls Charlotte’s ladylike style. But the collection is designed for women who want those fashion moments at prices that feel realistic.

One of the biggest runway statements comes from the shoes: gladiator heels. Strappy, bold, and a little unexpected, they give the softer clothes an edge. Davis laughs when I mention how quickly the audience noticed them.

“They’re fun, right?” she says. “A great shoe changes everything. You can wear a simple dress, add a gladiator heel, and suddenly the whole look feels modern.”

The heels bring just enough drama, grounding the collection in a current trend while keeping it wearable. They are the kind of piece that makes an outfit feel styled, even if the rest of the look is effortless.

And then there’s the color everyone is talking about: green. From fresh spring shades to deeper, richer tones, green appears throughout the collection as the season’s standout hue. Davis lights up when I ask about it.

“Green feels fresh,” she says. “It feels optimistic. It works on so many women, and it’s a beautiful way to bring color into your wardrobe without feeling too loud.”

On the runway, green reads as both classic and new — especially in dresses and tops that could easily become everyday favorites. It is a smart choice for a Southern fashion audience, where color is welcomed but elegance still matters.

What makes Davis’s approach compelling is that she is not trying to sell women an impossible version of themselves. There is no demand to be a size zero, no insistence that style requires discomfort, and no suggestion that fashion belongs only to celebrities. Her message is simple: women deserve clothes that make them feel good, at prices they can actually consider.

As we talk, it becomes clear that Davis is thinking about the women who will take these pieces home from Belk and make them part of real life. She mentions fit, comfort, versatility, and price as often as she mentions color or trend. For her, affordable fashion is not a compromise — it is the point.

“I love the idea that someone can find a dress she feels beautiful in and not feel guilty about buying it,” Davis says. “That matters.”

Before she leaves, I ask what she hopes women feel when they wear the line. She pauses for a moment, then smiles.

“Confident,” she says. “Pretty. Like themselves — just a little more polished.”

In Atlanta, where the Belk runway has just turned into a celebration of real-world glamour, that answer feels exactly right. Kristin Davis may always be linked to one of television’s most fashionable shows, but her new collection is less about fantasy closets and more about everyday style — the kind with a flattering dress, a great green shade, and maybe a pair of gladiator heels to make the whole day feel a little more fabulous.

## Kristin Davis brings Charlotte-approved polish to Belk with new fashion line

Kristin Davis may be forever linked to one of television’s most polished dressers, but her latest fashion move is aimed at women whose lives are a little less scripted — and whose bodies don’t all fit a sample size.

**Carrie’s Closet, Charlotte’s Price Tag**

There are few cultural forces as responsible for making women believe they needed a designer shoe budget as *Sex and the City*. The show did not merely introduce Manolo Blahniks to the mainstream; it practically handed them a recurring role, a backstory, and better lighting than some of the boyfriends.

Carrie Bradshaw made fashion feel like emotional oxygen: tulle for errands, stilettos for heartbreak, a baguette bag for every existential crisis. The fantasy was intoxicating. The math, less so. Somehow, a freelance columnist in Manhattan became the unofficial patron saint of “I’ll just put it on the card,” inspiring a generation to gaze longingly at designer windows while eating dinner at home to “save money,” a strategy that never quite produced enough for couture.

But if Carrie sold the dream, Charlotte York—polished, optimistic, and always dressed as though a thank-you note might be required—offered something more wearable. Charlotte’s style was ladylike without being dull: fit-and-flare dresses, pretty prints, tidy cardigans, the occasional pearl, and an unwavering belief that looking pulled together could count as a life philosophy.

Enter Kristin Davis, Charlotte herself, with a refreshingly democratic answer to the designer dilemma: fashion for women who enjoy looking elegant but do not wish to remortgage anything. Through Belk, Davis offered budget-friendly dresses, shoes, and swimsuits that channeled the Charlotte sensibility without the Park Avenue price tag.

It was a smart move, and frankly, very Charlotte. The collection leaned into femininity—flattering silhouettes, cheerful colors, soft prints, and clothes made for actual social occasions beyond “standing dramatically in front of a brownstone.” The dresses had that brunch-to-baby-shower versatility Charlotte would approve of. The shoes were pretty without requiring a pain management plan. The swimsuits suggested poolside poise rather than “I am on a yacht with a Russian artist and a complicated emotional arc.”

What made the line appealing was not that it tried to mimic the wild high-fashion fever dream of *Sex and the City*. It didn’t ask shoppers to cosplay as Carrie sprinting through Manhattan in heels that cost more than a sofa. Instead, it bottled a more attainable kind of glamour: neat, feminine, romantic, and just a little bit hopeful. In other words, Charlotte in retail form.

And the timing felt especially apt around the continued *Sex and the City* afterlife, including the 2010 sequel, *Sex and the City 2*. That film was many things: a travel fantasy, a costume parade, a desert mirage of wardrobe changes, and, depending on whom you ask, evidence that even beloved franchises should occasionally be offered a glass of water and a quiet sit-down. But visually, it doubled down on the series’ central promise: fashion as spectacle, fashion as identity, fashion as the loudest person in the room.

Against that backdrop, Davis’s Belk offerings felt almost radical in their practicality. While the film sent the women into ever more extravagant style territory, Davis was giving shoppers something they could actually buy, wear, and not have to explain to a credit counselor. It was aspirational, yes—but the aspiration was less “own a closet insured by Lloyd’s of London” and more “look lovely at dinner and still afford dinner.”

That may be the enduring fashion lesson of *Sex and the City*. Carrie made us dream bigger; Charlotte reminded us to tailor the dream. Designer fashion became the glittering horizon, always just one paycheck, one sample sale, or one financial delusion away. But Kristin Davis’s Belk line offered a gentler proposition: you can have charm, polish, and a little romantic flourish without needing a Vogue editor’s expense account.

In a world still recovering from the idea that shoes can be a personality, that feels like a happy ending Charlotte herself would believe in.

Davis’s Atlanta outfit felt like a modern cousin of that idea. The plaid skirt and belt had the office-ready structure, while the gladiator heels added a flash of confidence and flirtation. That idea felt refreshingly practical. Rather than designing for a fantasy version of womanhood, Davis seemed interested in the actual women who get dressed every morning: women with different shapes, budgets, routines, and insecurities. The emphasis was on fit, confidence, and accessibility.

Kristin Davis understands the power of fashion fantasy—but she seems just as committed to making sure real women can feel beautiful in clothes that actually work for them.
